# The least Mahler measure in the divisible group generated by conjugates of primitive Salem units

<a id="statement"></a>
## A lower bound from each Salem number occurring in a product

Let \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r>1\) be distinct primitive Salem generators, with \(r\ge1\).
Here a Salem number has degree at least four, and primitivity means that it generates, modulo signs, the group of units of relative norm one to its trace field.
Write \(d_i=[\mathbb Q(\alpha_i):\mathbb Q]\), and for each \(i\) choose one root \(a\) from each of the \(d_i/2\) inverse pairs of its minimal polynomial.
Denote these chosen roots by \(\mathcal A_i\).
Take integers \(n\ge1\) and \(c_a\in\mathbb Z\), a root of unity \(\xi\), and any \(w\) satisfying
\[
                         w^n=\xi u,\qquad
            u=\prod_{i=1}^r\ \prod_{a\in\mathcal A_i} a^{c_a}.            \tag{1}
\]
The union of the chosen sets is multiplicatively independent modulo roots of unity, so \(w\) is nontorsion exactly when some exponent is nonzero.
Put \(d_w=[\mathbb Q(w):\mathbb Q]\).
For each used index \(i\), define
\[
                      q_i=\frac{d_w}{n d_i}
                                   \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_i}|c_a| .
\]
Then \(q_i\) is a positive integer and, for nontorsion \(w\), the total logarithmic Mahler measure satisfies
\[
                m(w)\ \ge\ \max_{i\ {\rm used}} q_i\log\alpha_i
                       \ \ge\ \max_{i\ {\rm used}}\log\alpha_i .          \tag{2}
\]
Consequently the least positive total measure in the entire group (1), allowing all exponents, roots and torsion factors, is exactly \(\min_i\log\alpha_i\).
For an arbitrary nonempty family of distinct primitive Salem generators, the corresponding infimum is the infimum of their logarithms, since each product has finite support.
The trace fields may intersect or coincide, and the degrees and their permutation groups are unrestricted within the Salem hypotheses.

<a id="projection"></a>
## Relative norm projections for roots from different inverse pairs

Work in a finite Galois extension \(S/\mathbb Q\) containing \(w,\xi\) and all the conjugates of the given Salem numbers.
For an oriented root \(a\) put \(t_a=a+a^{-1}\), \(B_a=\mathbb Q(t_a)\), \(K_a=\mathbb Q(a)\) and \(\Delta_a=t_a^2-4\).
Thus \(B_a\) is totally real, \(K_a=B_a(\sqrt{\Delta_a})\) is quadratic, and exactly one real embedding of \(B_a\) sends \(\Delta_a\) to a positive value.
At this embedding the two values of \(a\) are \(\alpha_i,\alpha_i^{-1}\).
At all others the radicand is strictly negative.

For \(a,b\) from different inverse pairs, including pairs belonging to distinct inputs, we claim
\[
                            N_{S/K_a}(b)=1 .                              \tag{3}
\]
The compositum \(T=B_aB_b\) is totally real.
Each radicand is negative at some embedding of \(T\), so neither is a square there.
To compare their square classes, consider the sets of \(g\in G=\operatorname{Gal}(S/\mathbb Q)\) with \(g(\Delta_a)>0\) and \(g(\Delta_b)>0\), respectively.
They are nonempty left cosets of the subgroups fixing \(B_a\) and \(B_b\), since each positivity condition specifies exactly one embedding on its trace field.
If the cosets differ, the signs disagree at some embedding of \(T\), making \(\Delta_a/\Delta_b\) a nonsquare in \(T\).
If they agree, the two stabilizers agree, giving \(B_a=B_b=T\) with the same marked real embedding.
Equality of square classes in this case would give \(K_a=K_b\).
Apply a common embedding into \(\mathbb R\) above the marked place.
In the resulting real Salem field, each of the two inputs is recovered as the value greater than one among its generator and inverse.
Each recovered input generates the same relative norm-one group modulo signs, since the common trace field and the quadratic involution agree.
There is only one such primitive generator with positive value greater than one, so the two input numbers must agree.
Their traces under the common embedding are now the same value \(\alpha_i+\alpha_i^{-1}\), and injectivity gives \(t_a=t_b\), contradicting that their inverse pairs differ.
Thus the square classes differ also in the equal-coset case.

It follows that \(T(\sqrt{\Delta_a})\) and \(T(\sqrt{\Delta_b})\) are distinct quadratic extensions of \(T\).
Adjoining \(b\) to \(K_aT\) is still quadratic, and its nontrivial automorphism sends \(b\) to \(b^{-1}\), giving norm exactly one.
Transitivity of norms up to \(S\) and down to \(K_a\) proves (3).
Within the pair of \(a\) itself, the norm of the chosen orientation from \(S\) is \(a^{[S:K_a]}\).
Applying the norm to a putative torsion relation among chosen roots therefore isolates each exponent and forces it to vanish.
This proves the claimed joint multiplicative independence.

<a id="orthogonality"></a>
## Orthogonality of the logarithms and a contraction for each full set of conjugates

Write \(X_a(g)=\log|g(a)|\) on the finite group \(G\) with uniform probability.
For a second root \(b\) from a different inverse pair, the mean of \(X_b\) on any coset \(g\operatorname{Gal}(S/K_a)\) is \(\log|g(N_{S/K_a}b)|/[S:K_a]=0\) by (3).
Since \(X_a\) is constant on that coset, \(\mathbb E(X_aX_b)=0\).
For \(a\in\mathcal A_i\), its only nonzero values are \(\pm\log\alpha_i\), each occurring with probability \(1/d_i\).
In particular \(\mathbb E|X_a|=2\log\alpha_i/d_i\), \(\mathbb E X_a^2=2(\log\alpha_i)^2/d_i\), and \(\operatorname{sgn}(X_a)=X_a/\log\alpha_i\), taking \(\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0\).

For a fixed \(i\), the nonzero supports of the \(X_a\), \(a\in\mathcal A_i\), are pairwise disjoint, since \(g\) permutes distinct inverse pairs and there is only one pair of that Salem input off the unit circle.
Thus \(Y_i=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_i}\operatorname{sgn}(c_a)\operatorname{sgn}(X_a)\) has \(|Y_i|\le1\).
Using orthogonality against every other coordinate gives
\[
   \mathbb E\left|\log|g(u)|\right|
     \ \ge\ \mathbb E\left(Y_i(g)\sum_b c_b X_b(g)\right)
     \ =\ \frac{2\log\alpha_i}{d_i}\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_i}|c_a| .         \tag{4}
\]
This is an \(L^1\) contraction for the projection of the logarithmic sum onto the whole \(i\)-th set of conjugates, whose own \(L^1\) norm is the right side.
All roots and \(w\) are algebraic units, by (1) and the same equation for \(w^{-1}\).
For an algebraic unit the [absolute logarithmic height](../audits/literature/Smy08/Yin_U001.md#smy08-height-normalization) is half the mean absolute logarithm of the conjugate moduli, by their product one.
Since \(n\log|g(w)|=\log|g(u)|\), (4) implies \(m(w)=d_w h(w)\ge q_i\log\alpha_i\).

<a id="integral"></a>
## The orbit multiplicities are integers after taking an arbitrary root

Reverse the orientation of each root carrying a negative exponent, so that the supported oriented roots now have positive coefficients.
The group \(H=\operatorname{Gal}(S/\mathbb Q(w))\) fixes the signed exponent vector in (1).
Indeed its action on \(u\) changes \(u\) only by a root of unity, and the joint independence just proved makes comparison of the exponents valid after expressing the images in the chosen orientations.
It follows that \(H\) permutes each input's supported oriented roots, with no pair represented twice and with coefficients constant on each orbit.

For one such orbit \(O\), fix \(a\in O\), denote its coefficient by \(c>0\), and put \(E=\mathbb Q(w)K_a\).
Then \(|O|=[E:\mathbb Q(w)]\).
The unit \(v=N_{E/K_a}(w)\in K_a\) satisfies
\[
                       v^{n[S:E]}=\eta\,a^{c[S:K_a]}                      \tag{5}
\]
for a root of unity \(\eta\in K_a\), by (3), (1) and norm transitivity.
Applying \(N_{K_a/B_a}\) to (5) makes \(N_{K_a/B_a}(v)\) a root of unity.
It equals one, since \(B_a\) is totally real and the relative norm of any nonzero element is positive at each real place that becomes complex in \(K_a\).
There is at least one such place in every Salem field under consideration.
By primitivity \(v=\pm a^j\) for an integer \(j\).
This rank-one norm kernel description also applies in degree four.
The unit ranks in signatures \((2,d_i/2-1)\) and \((d_i/2,0)\) differ by one, the norm image contains all squares of trace-field units, and the real embedding gives only the torsion \(\{\pm1\}\).
These are the [primitive relative-unit argument](Yin_C_G0901_v44.md#units) and the [signature calculation](Yin_C_G0901_v45.md#extensions) transported to the conjugate field \(K_a\).
Since \(a\) is nontorsion, comparing exponents in (5) gives the positive integer
\[
                         j=\frac{c[E:K_a]}n .
\]
For each used \(i\), summing over its \(H\)-orbits gives
\[
              \sum_{O} j
               =\sum_O \frac{c\,d_w\,|O|}{n d_i}
               =\frac{d_w}{n d_i}\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_i}|c_a|
               =q_i .
\]
Here \(d_w|O|=[E:\mathbb Q]=d_i[E:K_a]\) in each summand.
Thus \(q_i\) is at least the number of its supported orbits, proving (2).
The smallest input \(\alpha_i\) belongs to the group and realizes the stated least measure.
This determines the infimum for the divisible group of the specified conjugates, while the existence of Salem numbers tending to one and the unrestricted Lehmer gap remain open.
